title: Isomorphism
body:
A [[Homomorphism]] that is also a bijection. Written $G \cong G'$, and it means the two groups
are **the same group wearing different labels**: relabel the elements by $\varphi$ and the
operation tables become identical.

If an isomorphism exists then every structural fact transfers. Same order, same number of
elements of each order, abelian if and only if the other is, same subgroup lattice. The things
that do **not** transfer are the things that were never structural: what the elements are made
of, what the operation is called, how you write them down.

```
Z_4 = {0,1,2,3} under +          <i> = {1, i, -1, -i} under ×
    0 ↦ 1
    1 ↦ i           φ(a + b) = φ(a)·φ(b)
    2 ↦ -1          addition of exponents  =  multiplication of powers
    3 ↦ -i
one group, two costumes
```

The general case of that example: $\mathbb{Z}_n \cong \mu_n$, the $n$th [[Roots of Unity]], and
it is the whole content of [[Cyclic Group]]'s classification. Adding indices mod $n$ and
multiplying unit-circle points are the same operation.

$\exp: (\mathbb{R}, +) \to (\mathbb{R}^{>0}, \times)$ is the other standard one, since
$e^{a+b} = e^a e^b$. It is why logarithms turn multiplication into addition, a fact that once
justified an entire industry of slide rules.

## Proving two groups are not isomorphic

The useful direction. You cannot check all $n!$ bijections, so you find an **invariant** they
disagree on:

| Invariant | Example |
|---|---|
| order of the group | trivially |
| abelian or not | $\mathbb{Z}_6 \cong \mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_3$ but $\mathbb{Z}_6 \not\cong S_3$, both order 6 |
| number of elements of order $k$ | $\mathbb{Z}_4$ has one element of order 2, $\mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_2$ has three |
| cyclic or not | $\mathbb{Z}_4$ is, $\mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_2$ is not |
| subgroup structure | orders and how many of each |

The order-6 pair is the one to remember: **there are exactly two groups of order 6**, one abelian
and one not, and the non-abelian one is $S_3 = D_3$.

## "The same up to relabelling" is a CS idea too

Isomorphism is what "structurally identical" means when you want to state it precisely rather
than gesture at it, and the vault has the idea in three other places:

- **[[Simulation]]** in [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]]: one machine imitating another. A DFA
  and the NFA it was built from are not isomorphic as machines, but they recognise the same
  language, which is the weaker equivalence the course actually cares about. Isomorphism is the
  strict version: the machines have the same shape, not just the same behaviour.
- **Graph isomorphism**: two [[Graph|graphs]] are the same graph if the vertices can be relabelled
  to match. Deciding it is famously neither known to be in P nor known to be [[NP-Complete]].
- **[[Abstraction]]**: naming a structure by its behaviour and treating implementations that share
  it as interchangeable is the same instinct one floor down, and is what an [[Interface]] declares.

Cayley's theorem is the biggest isomorphism statement in the course: every finite group is
isomorphic to a [[Subgroup]] of a [[Symmetric Group]]. Nothing exists that is not already a
[[Permutation Group]] in disguise.
